items.title: Pick Up Where You Left Off
items.description: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. Think about something that you loved doing when you were younger. Maybe you drew, played an instrument, wrote stories, or spent hours learning about something just because it fascinated you. Then school got busier, work took over, or the hobby started to feel less useful than everything else that was competing for your time. In 2023, David Brooks wrote an Atlantic article about people entering a new stage of life after their primary career. Many realized that, on the way up the professional ladder, they had abandoned interests and ambitions that had once mattered to them. In their 60s, they began picking up those lost strands. “The human hunger for meaning and fulfillment is strong,” Brooks wrote. “We shouldn’t have to wait until we’re 65 to learn how to transform our lives.” Returning to an old interest can remind you what it feels like to do something without needing it to lead anywhere. The point is not to re-create your childhood but to make room for interests that don’t fit neatly into the life you’ve already built. This weekend, return to something that you had quietly stopped doing. Pick up the book, racket, paintbrush, or instrument. You may find that you’ve indeed outgrown it—or wonder why you ever put it down. On Returning to What You Love The New Old Age By David Brooks What a new life stage can teach the rest of us about how to find meaning and purpose—before it’s too late ( From 2023 ) Read the article. How to Be Happy Growing Older By Arthur C. Brooks Your future will probably be better than your past. ( From 2023 ) Read the article. The Curious Personality Changes of Older Age By Faith Hill When people lose the ability to control their circumstances, their selves sometimes evolve instead. ( From 2023 ) Read the article. Still Curious? What I wish I’d known when I was younger : Last year, Arthur C. Brooks argued that the three reasons old people are happier can work for any age. Semi-retirees know the key to work-life balance : More and more older adults are working—in large part because they want to, Kate Cray wrote in 2023. Other Diversions Watching Tim Curry have fun was the most fun thing. What a bicentennial baby knows A turning point in AI writing PS Courtesy of Dennis L. My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “The bristlecone; awe on a multi-millennial scale,” Dennis L. writes. We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. Reply to this email with a photo and a short description. — Rafaela

items.title: The Terrible Movie That Chinese Audiences Can’t Stop Watching
items.description: One of the only compliments I can offer the new Chinese animated film Niu Lai is that it certainly qualifies as a film. There is sound. The pictures move. But beyond the basics of what makes a movie a movie, Niu Lai , which translates to “The Ox Comes,” contains little artistic merit. The plot, about a calf coming of age with the help of a leopard, a bird, and his mother, is thin, and the characters have been so nightmarishly rendered on a rudimentary computer program that they might as well be sleep-paralysis demons. Yet Niu Lai has become a bona fide box-office hit in China. Since a small distributor unceremoniously dumped it in theaters in early August, the film has become one of the most lucrative movies in Chinese history, making more than $7 million off a reported budget of no more than $500 and outperforming recent blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day . Much of its success is thanks to Chinese social media, where clips of it first went viral: Some users have embraced Niu Lai as a meme, purchasing tickets so they could ridicule the baffling work with an audience. Others have championed the project as anti-AI art, arguing that it deserves to be appreciated as a purely human creation. As flawed as Niu Lai may be, to the fans, it’s at least better than AI slop. I’m not so sure about that. Watching a bootleg version of Niu Lai felt painful but apt: What better way was there to see a jankily made film than in potato quality on my computer at home? Instead, what’s distinctly human about Niu Lai comes from everything around it: how it was made, how it became a sensation, and how it has inspired further creativity in turn. Theater workers have drawn posters by hand to help advertise the movie. Businesses have made plush toys of the bovine hero. Fans have donned cow masks for screenings, and although the film isn’t available in the United States, underground viewings have popped up in major cities. As such, Niu Lai is the rare passion project that has attracted audiences not because it’s so bad that it’s good, but because it’s an occasion to celebrate the ability to have an original idea at all. [ Read: Why a Chinese animated film has made more money than any Star Wars sequel ] Never mind that the idea was apparently underdeveloped from the start. The first-time director, Xin Yumeng, explained in an interview that he wanted to write about an ox because that’s his father’s zodiac symbol; the year he began working on it also happened to be 2021, the year of the ox. Production took five years, as the then-29-year-old Xin and his mother, Sun Lifang, wrote the screenplay together and made up the entire crew and cast: Sun sang the theme song, and Xin animated the 86-minute film frame by frame on SketchUp, an architectural-modeling program. The process was grueling, Xin said, adding that he kept going in part because he saw the story as a way to inspire viewers to not tang ping , or “lie flat,” referring to a societal trend in 2021 where young people in China rejected overworking by cheekily glorifying the act of lying down. In some ways, the movie is a deeply Chinese phenomenon: Fuzzy cartoon characters tend to become popular in the country— Zootopia 2 is the highest-grossing Hollywood film ever released there—and the words niu lai could also refer to the coming of a bull market, which has led some Chinese stock investors to purchase tickets for good luck. Plus, Niu Lai ’s threadbare plot is rooted in the principle of filial piety, as the titular protagonist learns to respect and care for his mother. The Niu Lai phenomenon also seems to embody a phrase that’s gained traction lately in China: huo ren gan , which, translated literally, means “alive-human feeling.” The film expresses this quality, but not only because Xi didn’t use AI to help create it. What makes Niu Lai stand out most is its unabashed sincerity. It is an earnest attempt to tell a fable about a naive cow, and the story of its making is deeply charming: Here is a mother-son duo, total outsiders to the entertainment industry, trying their best to turn their quixotic idea into reality. Making a movie anywhere requires overcoming so many hurdles that have nothing to do with art or creativity; there are budgets to be balanced and business expectations to be met. But Niu Lai is a modest reminder that any film simply begins with an idea and an irrepressible urge to see it through.

items.title: A New Way of Seeing Alien Worlds
items.description: Tomorrow morning, if all goes to plan, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, its latest and greatest orbital observatory, will lift off from its launchpad and add a little rocket-booster light to the Florida sunshine. A lot is riding on this mission. If the Roman is successful, it could give humanity a new way to see the planets around other stars and a fresh understanding of the largest-scale objects that we know to exist. But if it fails, NASA’s science program, which is already fending off ruinous budget cuts , will need to seriously rethink its future. The Artemis mission to the moon was a big win for human spaceflight, and now the science side of the house badly needs one. NASA’s engineers have spent more than a decade readying the Roman for this moment. Before the telescope arrived in Florida, it spent more than a year in NASA’s largest clean room at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. To get near it, you had to be mummified alive. When I visited in December, NASA staffers led me to a sterile, fluorescent-lit locker room. They tossed me a white jumpsuit and two sets of booties with tight-fitting straps. They told me to put on a beard net and hair net, and triple-wrapped the gap between my jumpsuit sleeves and gloves with blue tape. The astronomers didn’t want my skin exposed in the clean room. Dry flakes of it could drift off and settle onto the telescope’s ultrasmooth primary mirror. “You’re going to be the dirtiest thing in here,” one of them told me, as we walked through a little chamber where more than 30 nozzles blasted us with air. I jotted down this remark on special mint-green paper that sheds fewer particulates than a regular notebook, and then stepped into a cavernous eight-story white space soundtracked by the hum of six school-bus-size fans. At its center, the Roman stood more than 40 feet high, and it was surrounded by more than a dozen people, all in identical jumpsuits. Half were standing in clusters, talking, while the other half were up on motorized lifts, fussing with the telescope, applying duct tape and making final adjustments. More than a thousand people have worked on this project, and those who are lucky enough to get close to the hardware seem to derive a physical pleasure from the experience. [ Read: Inside Donald Trump’s attack on NASA’s science missions ] The Roman has a pretty shady backstory for a scientific instrument. Its primary mirror was part of a surprise gift bestowed on NASA by the National Reconnaissance Office. The NRO is one of America’s most secretive government agencies, and it apparently had a Hubble-class spare just lying around. A cash-strapped agency can’t afford to be too choosy about provenance: NASA took this mirror that was supposed to point down at the ground , for surveillance, and will instead point it out at the stars. Coronagraph delivery and unboxing (Chris Gunn / NASA) The NRO’s spare mirror has also solved a bit of internal politics for NASA’s science program. The Roman is built to monitor the universe at the very largest scales, to map the cosmic superstructure of galaxy clusters that stretches out from us in every direction, to see how it has expanded over time. These observations might lead scientists to a more refined sense for gravity, and may even help them discover new physics. But the idea for a mission like this was originally conceived of around the early 2000s, shortly after the discovery of dark energy , and a survey of the large-scale universe seemed like the obvious next thing to do. When NASA was finally ready to build the telescope, in the early 2010s, the action in astronomy had shifted closer to home. Scientists were in the midst of discovering thousands of new planets around nearby stars, and they wanted to find more. Although the Roman’s original mission plan did allow for some planet-hunting, the new mirror would allow them to do it in a whole new way. [ Read: The Nobel Prize winner who thinks we have the universe all wrong ] Finding a little world with its own atmosphere in the glare of a nearby star is tricky work. Even the very largest planets will be a billion times fainter than the suns they orbit. When I spoke with Dominic Benford, Roman’s program scientist at NASA Headquarters, he likened the challenge to spotting a firefly buzzing around a powerful searchlight from thousands of miles away. To make this possible, astronomers have lodged an exquisite new kind of coronagraph into the Roman’s metallic guts. Coronagraphs originally helped astronomers see the plasma flares emanating from our sun, by blocking out the far more brilliant light from the solar disk. In a sense, the device creates a brief artificial eclipse inside the telescope. The Roman’s coronagraph is designed to do something similar for more distant stars so that astronomers can see the planets that surround them. When the telescope is trained on a star in our Milky Way, it will catch a lot of light, and then run it through the coronagraph’s system of barriers and mirrors. Two of the mirrors that it uses may be even more beautiful in their design than the ultrasmooth, eight-foot primary. Each is smaller than the average makeup compact, and has more than 1,600 actuators that can individually deform tiny portions of the glass in tiny increments, less than the diameter of a helium atom. Astronomers will employ hundreds of these warping movements, spread across the mirrors, to deflect a specific star’s glare, creating an image of the star within a ring of nearly pure darkness. Deformable mirrors like these have previously been used on the ground to help telescopes see through the warble and blur of Earth’s atmosphere. But no one has ever sent one of this complexity to space. The Roman team believes that up there, where the viewing conditions are more pristine, the Roman will be able to deliver the first direct images of distant planets in visible light. Until now, most of the extrasolar planets that scientists have observed have been detected indirectly. In some cases, a planet’s existence is inferred from the gravitational force that it exerts on its host star, causing the star to wobble. Or astronomers might see a host star dim, repeatedly and predictably, as an orbiting planet passes in front of it. We have been able to get direct snapshots of only a few young planets that were still roiling hot and glowing brightly, and mainly in infrared. The Roman telescope’s coronagraph should be able to see worlds that aren’t glowing at all. Like Earth, they will be illuminated solely by the soft visible light of their host stars. [ Read: When a telescope is a national-security risk ] I asked Vanessa Bailey, the coronagraph’s instrument technologist, if there were any particular stars that she was excited to inspect. Because the coronagraph isn’t part of the telescope’s main mission, just three of the first 18 months will be set aside for its observations. Bailey said that the astronomers will use that time to look at previously detected planets that are only tens of light-years away. She mentioned the Epsilon Eridani system, where a Jupiter-size world is known to orbit an orange dwarf star. With the coronagraph, they’ll stare at it for many hours, letting photons from the planet slowly pile up. “It’s just going to be a little fuzzy smudge, just barely there,” Bailey said. “But we might be able to tell if it’s cloudy or clear, and we might be able to say whether it’s more like Jupiter or Neptune.” All of this could go wrong. Bailey told me that the coronagraph has never been tested outside the lab, and in space, it may not work. If for some reason the mirrors are misaligned, or the instrument malfunctions, any planets would be lost in the astral glare. NASA’s long-running quest to find another living world in the universe would be set back, perhaps by a decade or more. But if the coronagraph does fulfill its mission, it will serve as a proof of concept for NASA’s next really big telescope, the Habitable Worlds Observatory, which the agency has been developing for more than a decade. Roman’s coronagraph will be able to find only large planets—Saturn-size or ideally bigger—that circle their stars in chilly, distant orbits. NASA scientists want to place a much more precise one on the HWO. That mission will fixate on more than 100 nearby stars that share the sun’s rough age and brightness. Its coronagraph will cast a much tighter ring of near darkness around them, to see if any planets show up in the closer, warmer orbits that might be more hospitable to life—and it will even look for signs of life in the planets’ atmospheres. But the HWO won’t lift off until the late 2030s at the earliest. For now, the Roman has to prove out. It has to survive the violence of launch and fly a million miles from Earth so that its mirrors can catch the light of a nearby star and then surround it in darkness so deep that a faint alien world appears.

items.title: Tentative de mutinerie au Niger : Le Ministère de la Défense annonce avoir repris le contrôle de la situation
items.description: Un incident militaire a secoué la capitale nigérienne, Niamey, ce samedi 29 août 2026. Selon un communiqué officiel lu à la Télévision nationale, un groupe de soldats « en rupture avec le règlement militaire » a fait usage de ses armes dans plusieurs sites stratégiques de la ville, avant d'être maîtrisé par les forces républicaines. D'après les informations délivrées par le ministre de la Défense nationale, le Général d'armée Salifou Mody, le mouvement a débuté au sein de la caserne de la base 101 de Niamey. Les militaires mutins ont dans un premier temps séquestré certains de leurs camarades avant d'étendre leurs actions à d'autres « sites sensibles » de la capitale, où des tirs ont été signalés. Face à cette situation, le communiqué précise que « la prompte réaction des Forces de défense et de sécurité » (les Forces Armées Nigériennes, FAN) a permis de « circonscrire ce mouvement d'humeur ». Les autorités affirment que le contrôle de ces sites est en train d'être « progressivement » repris, sans toutefois donner plus de détails sur la nature exacte des lieux visés ni sur l'état des forces en présence. Dans ce même message, le Ministère de la Défense su Niger a rassuré la population de Niamey et du pays. Il est demandé aux citoyens de « garder leur calme » et de « vaquer librement à leurs occupations », signalant que la situation est désormais sous contrôle et que la vie normale peut reprendre son cours. Minute.bf

items.title: Naqvi visits passport office at Karachi's Awami Markaz, says facility to be expanded
items.description: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Saturday visited the passport office at Karachi’s Awami Markaz and said the facility would be “expanded for citizens’ convenience”, according to his ministry. A statement by the Ministry of Interior said Naqvi met citizens who were at the centre to seek passports. He asked them about the time it took between the issuance of tokens and their turn at the counter. “Citizens appreciated the passport issuance system and expressed satisfaction,” the ministry said. According to the statement, they also told Naqvi that their work was completed within a few minutes. The citizens also told Naqvi that their work was completed within a few minutes. “No difficulty arose in getting the passport made, nor did they have to wait,” the interior ministry claimed, citing the applicants. In June, officials at Awami Markaz passport office were suspended after a foreign national was issued a Pakistani passport there. Naqvi also visited Jinnah International Airport, where the immigration system malfunctioned as he reviewed the process at the counters, the interior ministry said in a separate statement issued in the morning. The minister contacted relevant officials and directed them to immediately resolve the issue, stressing that arrangements for alternative measures should be ensured in case of such incidents. “The immigration process must not be halted under any circumstances,” Naqvi was quoted as saying. At the airport, the minister also met passengers who were departing for foreign countries and inquired about the immigration process. He ordered strict action against passengers with fake documents, adding that those with incomplete and unverified documents would not be allowed to travel under any circumstances. Naqvi had also visited Karachi in late July, when he met with President Asif Ali Zardari. The month prior, he paid a surprise visit to a mega centre of the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) in the Safoora Goth area. The interior minister’s remarks earlier this month ignited a fresh debate within political circles after he said the country’s governance system had “collapsed” and proposed to create new provinces. Later, he said the incumbent government would complete its constitutional term. Nisar Ahmed Khuhro of the PPP, which rules Sindh, had demanded Naqvi’s resignation and accused him of undermining the Constitution by “endorsing a hybrid system”.

items.title: 4e fenêtre éliminatoires Coupe du monde 2027 : duel Sénégal-Angola aujourd’hui à 18 h 30
items.description: Battus jeudi par l’Égypte, à l’occasion de leur première sortie dans cette quatrième fenêtre des éliminatoires de la Coupe du monde 2027, les Lions retrouvent le parquet de Dakar Arena, aujourd’hui. Ils seront opposés à l’Angola à partir de 18 h 30. Un sérieux adversaire pour le Sénégal qui devra impérativement réagir. Après cette défaite d’entrée, les deux derniers matches s’annoncent décisifs pour les Lions qui devront s’imposer pour conserver toutes leurs chances dans la course à la qualification. Avec désormais cinq victoires et deux défaites dans le groupe F, le Sénégal disputera son deuxième match de cette fenêtre, aujourd’hui, à 18 h 30, à Dakar Arena, face aux champions d’Afrique en titre. En effet, les coéquipiers de Brancou Badio qui abordaient ce tournoi sur une série de cinq victoires consécutives, doivent impérativement remporter leurs deux derniers matches contre l’Angola et le Mali après leur revers contre l’Égypte. A lire aussi : Éliminatoires Mondial 2027 de basket : l’Égypte s’impose face au Sénégal Menés de quatre points à l’issue du premier quart-temps, les Égyptiens ont su se ressaisir pour créer la plus grosse surprise parmi les six rencontres disputées jeudi à Dakar (Sénégal) et à Radès (Tunisie). Les Lions, qui ont complètement raté leur match, n’ont pu réussir que 24 tirs sur 70 tentatives. Le meneur de jeu Brancou Badio est sorti de sa zone de confort, manquant ses onze tentatives à 3 points. Il a terminé avec neuf points, son plus faible total depuis le début des Éliminatoires Zone Afrique. Le Sénégal a également été dominé au rebond, 53 à 45, dont un impressionnant total de 23 rebonds offensifs. Face à l’Angola ce samedi, le coach des Lions, DeSagana Diop, devra changer de système et rectifier certaines erreurs. Car l’équipe angolaise, qui fait partie des leaders de ce groupe F, a fait étalage de sa maîtrise défensive, laissant la RDC sans réponse, jeudi à Dakar Arena, lors de la journée d’ouverture des éliminatoires. Les champions d’Afrique en titre ont en effet pris un excellent départ, poussant les Congolais à perdre 22 ballons, un record, avant de s’imposer 100-68. Onze joueurs angolais ont réussi au moins une interception, Cleusio Castro menant la danse avec cinq. Avec 22 interceptions, l’Angola a battu son propre record des Éliminatoires Zone Afrique, établi lors du premier tour de la compétition, lorsqu’il avait terminé avec 21 interceptions lors de sa victoire 90-68 contre l’Ouganda. Absa NDONG

items.title: Houet : un enfant de 9 ans meurt par noyade au secteur 23
items.description: Houet : un enfant de 9 ans meurt par noyade au secteur 23 Bobo-Dioulasso, 28 août 2026 (AIB) – Un enfant de 9 ans, élève en classe de CE1, au secteur 23 de Bobo-Dioulasso, est mort par noyade, le jeudi 27 août 2026, après une forte pluie tombée dans la matinée, a constaté l’AIB. Selon les informations recueillies par l’AIB, le drame s’est produit aux abords du marigot traversant le village de Kiri et le secteur 23, en direction de Bama. D’après le père du défunt, l’enfant, Amza Traoré, profitait des vacances scolaires pour se rendre chaque matin dans un atelier de soudure. Il rentrait généralement à la mi-journée pour déjeuner avant de repartir à l’atelier. « Aujourd’hui, comme à son habitude, après être revenu déjeuner, il devait retourner à l’atelier. Étant moi-même en service hors de la ville, son oncle lui avait d’ailleurs demandé de rejoindre l’atelier sans tarder », a-t-il expliqué. Selon son récit, l’enfant s’est toutefois rendu vers le marigot en compagnie de trois camarades. C’est au cours de cette sortie qu’il serait tombé dans l’eau. Pris de panique, ses camarades auraient couru donner l’alerte au responsable de l’atelier, qui a aussitôt contacté les sapeurs-pompiers. Les secours ont retrouvé le corps de l’enfant aux environs de 17 heures, selon les informations recueillies sur place par l’AIB. Après les constatations de la police, la dépouille a été remise à la famille, en présence des propriétaires terriens et de plusieurs riverains. Agence d'Information du Burkina OA/AB/wis

items.title: No safe place
items.description: ALL the pen and paper in the world are insufficient to describe the pain and torture inflicted on women. In Pakistan, all flat surfaces could be covered with stories of women who have been harassed, beaten, tortured and killed. Few women in the country can claim to have lived a life free from male harassment. Today, we mourn yet another woman. Hina Javed was married to Faisal Asghar, a former professor with an alleged history of harassment, less than a year ago. She was found dead in the bathroom of the apartment she shared with her husband. Evidence at the scene pointed to a possible hanging. According to the FIR filed by Hina’s brother, there was proof of much more than that. It is reported that Hina was found with her hands tied. A wire was around her neck and tied to the shower rod. She also had a cloth stuffed in her mouth. The post-mortem found that she had a broken neck and injuries to her ribs, hips and lips. The findings showed that she had been tortured. Blood pooled around her heart, and there appeared to be some evidence that she had been poisoned. The investigation is still underway. Hina’s husband has been arrested, and court proceedings are underway. Sadly, in this society, harassment of women is not taken seriously; women are seldom believed when they file complaints against their harassers or dangerous stalkers. It is no wonder that many of them are convinced that nothing will come of it, that, in fact, the victim will be blamed for inviting the attention of such criminals, who routinely include murderers. Even if such criminals are nabbed and arrested, they walk into court with no remorse, their chests outstretched, their sense of entitlement and arrogance preceding them. The tragedy is that so many of them are walking around Pakistan today. Judging from the regularity with which husbands, fathers and brothers torture or kill women, it can safely be said that millions of men in Pakistan think that they are justified in their role as judge, jury and executioner. Millions of Pakistani women suffer abuse. It is too late for Hina Javed. But there are millions of other Pakistani women who are enduring similar conditions and who could be saved from their torture. According to UNFPA, 28 per cent of all Pakistani women and 34pc of married women say they have experienced some form of physical and sexual violence. This number is likely to be an underestimation because most women never report any abuse to the authorities, as they fear more violence or being shamed in society. Because of this underreporting, the available numbers tell an incomplete story. A recent aggregation of public reports on the issue was conducted by the NGO Saahil, which found that the total number of cases involving gender-based violence was 7,071 in 2025. This was an increase from the 5,253 registered a year earlier, showing that even without secure reporting protections and infrastructure, the numbers are growing. As is always the case in Pakistan, a few media outlets and social media posts took note of the issue, and then it was buried. The core of this tragedy is two-pronged. The first is that family and sociocultural structures keep women in violent relationships. The second is that there are hardly any places where women in these situations can go to be assured of safety and secrecy. There are legal issues that make the provision of a haven for abused women difficult. Existing provisions in the law make it possible for courts to order that women be retur­ned to their legal gu­­a­rdians when, in fact, these very guardians may be the ones abusing the women in the first place. The ability of wo­­m­en to help other wo­­men is hindered by the fact that most live in family structures dominated by men where they are unable to help their friends, family or neighbours who they know are being abused. The result is cases like Hina Javed’s. It is heartening that First Lady Aseefa Bhutto has taken an interest in the case, and one hopes that justice is served. It would be even better for politicians like her to focus on the structural and practical issues that survivors of domestic violence in Pakistan face when they try to escape from their abusive situations. Laws should be strong enough to stop women from being treated as property that courts can order to be returned to the ‘owners’. At the very least, there is a need for a large number of well-funded shelters that can ensure both secrecy and safety for abused women. Safe places are necessary so that no more dead women are found strangled in bathrooms. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. rafia.zakaria@gmail.com Published in Dawn, August 29th, 2026

items.title: Ouagadougou: environ 2 000 têtes d’animaux mises en fourrière en trois mois
items.description: La police municipale de Ouagadougou affirme avoir mis en fourrière, durant les trois dernier mois, juin, juillet et août 2026, environ 2 000 têtes d’animaux pour divagation dans la cité. «Face à la recrudescence du phénomène de la divagation des animaux dans la cité, la Direction de la Police de la Salubrité et de la Tranquillité Urbaine (DPSTU) de la Police Municipale de Ouagadougou mène quotidiennement des opérations de lutte contre ce fléau dans les différents quartiers de la ville. Durant la saison pluvieuse, période au cours de laquelle le phénomène prend davantage d’ampleur, la DPSTU a intensifié ses interventions afin de lutter efficacement contre la divagation des animaux et de préserver la sécurité, la salubrité et le cadre de vie des populations. Ainsi, au cours des trois derniers mois, notamment juin, juillet et août 2026, ce sont environ deux milles (2000) têtes d’animaux, composées de bovins, de chevaux, d’ovins et de caprins, qui ont été mises en fourrière. Au-delà des risques d’accidents et des nuisances qu’elle occasionne, la divagation des animaux constitue également une préoccupation en matière d’hygiène et de salubrité publique. Elle contribue notamment à la dégradation des espaces verts et à la destruction de la flore urbaine. La Police Municipale de Ouagadougou rappelle à la population l’importance du respect des textes en vigueur, notamment la Loi n°022-2005/AN portant Code de l’hygiène publique au Burkina Faso, ainsi que l’Arrêté n°97-027/MATS/PKAD/CO prescrivant les mesures d’hygiène et de salubrité dans la Ville de Ouagadougou. Elle invite, par conséquent, les propriétaires d’animaux à prendre toutes les dispositions nécessaires afin d’éviter leur divagation dans la ville. La Police Municipale, toujours plus proche de vous !» Service de l’Information et de la Communication NB: Le titre et le chapeau sont de la rédaction L’article Ouagadougou: environ 2 000 têtes d’animaux mises en fourrière en trois mois est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Pénurie d’eau embouteillée | Mais que fait le gouvernement ?
items.description: On n’avait jamais vu cela en Tunisie. C’est dégradant et humiliant : ces longues files d’attente devant les magasins et les supermarchés pour acheter de l’eau minérale embouteillée, ou encore cette vidéo circulant sur les réseaux sociaux et qui montre des citoyens dévalisant un camion transportant des bouteilles d’eau minérale opportunément bloquée dans un embouteillage, sans jeu de mot de mauvais goût. Si elle a prouvé quelque chose, cette pénurie en pleine canicule estivale a levé le voile, s’il en est encore besoin, sur l’incompétence crasse des gouvernants et l’arrogante indiscipline des gouvernés, souvent animés par l ' instinct et rarement par la raison. Latif Belhedi Pourtant, les unités tunisiennes de production et d’embouteillage d’eau minérale tournent à plein régime pour tenter de normaliser l’approvisionnement du marché, encore marqué par des pénuries dans de nombreux points de vente. C’est ce que ne cesse d’affirmer la Chambre syndicale nationale des producteurs de boissons non alcoolisées (affiliée à l’Utica), selon laquelle la demande a augmenté d’environ 30 % cet été par rapport aux niveaux habituels, principalement en raison des vagues de chaleur à répétition. À cette hausse exceptionnelle de la consommation se sont ajoutées des coupures d’électricité dans plusieurs régions du pays, entraînant l’arrêt temporaire des lignes d’embouteillage pour des durées variables. La conjonction de ces deux facteurs a également conduit à l’épuisement des stocks de sécurité constitués durant l’hiver précisément pour faire face au pic de la demande estivale. Cherchez les responsables ! La Chambre assure que la capacité de production nationale est désormais mobilisée au maximum et qu’un suivi continu de la situation est assuré grâce à des réunions entre les producteurs, le ministère du Commerce et du Développement des exportations, ainsi que l’Office national du thermalisme et de l’hydrothérapie. Les quantités disponibles sont acheminées vers les différentes régions en fonction des besoins, sous la supervision des directions régionales du Commerce, nous assure-t-on. Les producteurs rejettent par ailleurs les accusations, relayées notamment sur les réseaux sociaux, selon lesquelles une partie des bouteilles serait délibérément retenue pour alimenter la pénurie ou à des fins spéculatives. Selon la Chambre, une telle stratégie de stockage ne serait pas économiquement rentable, car la demande devrait diminuer progressivement avec la baisse des températures dans les semaines à venir, ramenant l’offre à un niveau supérieur aux besoins du marché. Les difficultés d’approvisionnement des consommateurs perdurent depuis plusieurs semaines et se sont révélées particulièrement marquées au cours d’un été également caractérisé par des interruptions fréquentes de la distribution d’eau potable. Le secteur compte actuellement 31 unités d’embouteillage, avec une capacité globale déclarée d’environ 520 000 bouteilles par heure. Ces derniers jours, le président Kaïs Saïed a visité des unités de production et d’embouteillage à Oueslatia, dans le gouvernorat de Kairouan, s’attardant notamment sur les difficultés liées à la distribution. Pour lui, le produit existe en quantités suffisantes, mais ce sont des spéculateurs qui provoquent les pénuries et complotent contre l'Etat. Depuis cette visite, la situation ne s’est pas améliorée, au contraire, la pénurie est devenue encore plus aiguë. C’est à se demander à quoi servent ces visites officielles qui sont rarement suivies de décisions concrètes qui aident à régler les problèmes constatés. Cela rappelle la célèbre phrase d’un ancien chef de gouvernement, Hamadi Jebali en l’occurrence, qui, en 2012, constatant les dysfonctionnements du système d’évacuation dans un quartier populaire de Tunis, s’était exclamé devant les caméras : «Mais que fait le gouvernement ?» C’est justement la question que se posent depuis toujours les Tunisiens sans y trouver de réponse. L’article Pénurie d’eau embouteillée | Mais que fait le gouvernement ? est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.description: Niamey, 29 août 2026 — Dans la nuit de vendredi a samedi 29 août, vers 1h20 du matin, un incident grave , impliquant un groupe d’éléments de la base 101 de Niamey a été signalé à Niamey perturbant le sommeil des citoyens. Selon un communiqué officiel rendu public aujourd’hui par le Ministre d’État, ministre de la Défense nationale, le Général d’armée Salifou Modi, des militaires en rupture avec les règles de discipline de l’armée ont séquestré certains de leurs camarades à l’intérieur de la caserne puis ouvert le feu sur plusieurs sites sensibles de la capitale. Le communiqué précise que, grâce à la réaction rapide et coordonnée des Forces de défense et de sécurité, le mouvement d’humeur a été circonscrit dans les meilleurs délais. Les autorités indiquent que les opérations engagées ont permis la reprise progressive du contrôle des emprises concernées et la neutralisation des foyers d’hostilités. Le Ministre d’État a salué la promptitude et le professionnalisme des unités intervenues et a assuré que l’ensemble des mesures nécessaires étaient prises pour rétablir définitivement l’ordre, identifier les instigateurs et engager les poursuites disciplinaires et judiciaires appropriées. Les autorités invitent la population au calme et à la prudence, tout en indiquant que la situation est désormais totalement sous contrôle. Les services de sécurité appellent également à faire confiance aux informations officielles et à éviter la diffusion de rumeurs susceptibles d’altérer la quiétude publique. items.title: The Kennedy Center Has a Problem That Courts Can’t Fix
items.description: To put the legal fight over the Kennedy Center in operatic terms, it has become more than a little Wagnerian. After another hearing this week about another attempt to add Donald Trump’s name to its marble facade, the fate of the national cultural center remains grim and unresolved, and no finale is in sight. What could deliver a resolution? That’s still not clear, in part because the defendant in a long-running lawsuit—the Kennedy Center’s board of trustees—keeps making decisions that drag out the ordeal. A judge can restrain the board but has no power to remake it. Congress can remake it, but only through legislative action, which Trump can veto. And meanwhile, his board remains in place—able to make new decisions that invite new challenges that send the parties back to the same judge. In December, Trump’s allies on the Kennedy Center board—billionaires, White House aides, Fox News personalities, and other figures associated with Trump world—voted to add the president’s name to the building, and in March, they signed off on his plan to shut down the center for renovations. But by May, both actions had hit a wall: In a lawsuit filed by a Democratic member of Congress, Joyce Beatty, who serves as one of the board’s ex officio members, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper concluded that the board had exceeded its authority by renaming the Kennedy Center. He also found that its decision to close the center was likely a breach of the trustees’ fiduciary duties, describing that vote as “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” So they revoted this summer to close down, and they okayed a different plan to get Trump’s name back on the center’s exterior—in three places, actually, even though the relevant federal statute states that “no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas” of the complex. Whatever the merits of the renovation plan, the Kennedy Center is plainly in crisis. Trump’s takeover drove away artists, donors, and audiences; staff purges have stripped it of institutional memory. There is a reasonable argument that because its brand has become so repellent, the Kennedy Center might as well close temporarily so that tenants such as the National Symphony Orchestra can have a shot at recovery beyond its walls. But the ongoing litigation has exposed other concerns about the institution’s leadership, who include an executive team led by Matt Floca—whose expertise is in facilities, not arts management—and a board, the chair of which is Trump himself. Although boards at nonprofits are charged with oversight, this one has largely rubber-stamped proposals that have come before it. After Cooper ordered the board to take a more detailed look at the renovation proposal, it commissioned a new report from a commercial real-estate firm, JLL. (Five years ago, JLL was tapped to try to sell Trump’s Washington, D.C., hotel, though it backed out after the January 6 riot.) This week, Justice Department lawyers representing the board suggested in a court filing that the entire Kennedy Center complex might have to be “taken down” if the renovation plans are thwarted. Meanwhile, the Kennedy Center has gone largely silent. A tarp still hangs over the facade where Trump’s name was once fastened, a decision that critics have characterized as a petulant display of the president’s vanity. The board has argued in court filings that removing Trump’s name jeopardizes “hundreds of millions of dollars” in donations to a mysterious fundraising vehicle, which it created earlier this year. The board has provided no detailed accounting of how a two-year closure would affect ticket sales, fundraising, or artist relationships—even as reporting from The Washington Post this week revealed that the center’s finances have deteriorated dramatically since Trump’s name was put on the building, issues about which the board was informed. [ Read: Donald Trump’s new plan to get his name back on the Kennedy Center ] All of these actions have become central to the lawsuit brought by Beatty, whose lawyers have repeatedly criticized the Trump-appointed trustees for negligence and alleged that the board has misled the public. At the emergency hearing Thursday, Cooper spent nearly two hours questioning both sides, pressing Department of Justice lawyers on why they were rushing to reinstall the president’s name, which the center had said could happen as soon as September 8. (He also questioned whether he even had jurisdiction to stop the board, because in June, the Kennedy Center had appealed his earlier ruling.) Demonstrators made their frustration apparent as they filled the galleys and an overflow room for the hearing, which ended with Cooper requesting that the Kennedy Center extend the date for implementing its latest Trump-recognition plan while he weighs a decision. In a filing later that day, its lawyers agreed to hold off until at least October 8. The delay further prolongs the issue. But there are worse fates for the Kennedy Center, one staffer—speaking on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal—told me outside the courthouse: “A holding pattern is better than them taking a bulldozer to it.” Each new development and court filing in opposition makes the same structural problem clearer: A judge can restrain the board’s actions time and time again, but “if the problem is a governance problem, there is not much that a court can do,” John Harrison, a law professor at the University of Virginia, told me. The clearest path out of the cycle may instead run through Congress, which established the Kennedy Center as well as the board that governs it. Harrison described the institution’s governing body as something of a “black box” from a court’s perspective. A judge may issue orders to the people responsible for the entity and enforce those orders, but he generally will not reach inside that structure to prescribe how its decisions should be made when those procedures are established by statute. That leaves two options for lawmakers, he said. First, Congress could change the Kennedy Center’s governance structure. Alternatively, it could leave the board intact but alter the law governing what the board is permitted to do—for instance, by making the rules surrounding the Kennedy Center’s name more explicit. Any provisions affecting the Kennedy Center could conceivably hitch a ride in a larger legislative package rather than come to the floor as a stand-alone measure, Harrison said, but “it would have to be in a bill. It would have to be done by an act of Congress,” which, for now, seems unlikely. The issue is partly a product of the Kennedy Center’s unique governance structure. Congress charged the board with maintaining and administering it as both the national center for performing arts and a living memorial to President John F. Kennedy. Thirty-six members are appointed by the president to serve a six-year term, and another 23 serve as ex officio members by virtue of their government office, including the secretary of state; the librarian of Congress; the Smithsonian secretary; the mayor of Washington, D.C.; and the director of the National Park Service. In the past, presidents usually filled vacancies only for trustees who had reached the end of their term, which resulted in a bipartisan mix. But Trump broke with that practice after returning to office last year and firing Joe Biden–appointed trustees before their term was up. He then made another unprecedented move in becoming chairman—a role no other sitting president had previously held—and, along with his hand-picked board, injected an overtly partisan flavor into the institution. Historically, trustees did not run the Kennedy Center. Neither were they required to be arts professionals, Michael Kaiser, who served as the center’s president from 2001 to 2014, told me. Presidents could select trustees with ties to the Kennedy Center, expertise in the arts, philanthropic capacity, or none of the above, he said: “It’s a mix of people historically. We’ve had boards who are very responsible, very engaged with the staff leadership, very generous, but also representing a wide variety of backgrounds and experiences.” The board, he stressed, is a governing and oversight body, not a management one. If the current board members are not sufficiently engaged with the Kennedy Center’s problems, they’re not the first. Trustees were scrutinized during Kaiser’s tenure in 2005 by the Government Accountability Office, which released a report the following year about the Kennedy Center’s management of federally funded capital projects and weaknesses in board oversight. That included low trustee attendance, insufficient monitoring after the board had delegated substantial responsibility to management, and inadequate information to properly evaluate the implementation of capital projects—an observation that echoes what Cooper wrote in his May 29 decision about the current board’s vote to close the center. The GAO report also quoted one trustee who said that many members regarded their appointment as “honorific” and viewed donating and fundraising as their main responsibilities. Kaiser offered a more nuanced characterization: Many trustees were honored to serve, he said, and some made their greatest contribution financially—“but as a group, particularly through the leadership of the board, there was a sense of a requirement to govern the institution well.” When Trump remade the board shortly after returning to office last year, he appointed allies including Maria Bartiromo, Sergio Gor, Laura Ingraham, Susie Wiles, and Dan Scavino as general trustees. Second Lady Usha Vance, who had also been named a trustee last year, quietly stepped down recently without citing a reason . “The Second Lady spent a year on the board concluding her service on February 11, 2026,” her spokesperson wrote to me this week. “She is grateful to the President for her appointment and enjoyed her time with both the Kennedy Center and the Washington National Opera. She plans to continue being a patron of both organizations.” Lately, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick—whose wife serves as a trustee—has also joined Kennedy Center board meetings, “helping out” organizationally, he told me in June. And he appeared at the courthouse Thursday to defend the center’s new resolution while doubling down on its leaders’ warnings that the building would have to be demolished if the center could not raise enough money for repairs. [ Read: What I saw inside the Kennedy Center ] Since Trump’s takeover, his board has quickly begun exercising its authority in consequential—and ultimately legally contested—ways. Last year, I obtained documents that showed the board had amended its bylaws that May to designate ex officio trustees as nonvoting members. That left voting authority entirely with the presidentially appointed general trustees, clearing the way for them to unanimously add Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center in December. And in March of this year, the board approved Trump’s proposal to close the entire complex for roughly two years while it underwent renovations. (When Cooper ruled against the renaming this May, he also said the board could not prevent ex officio members from voting.) The scale of that closure warrants substantial board involvement, Kaiser said. During his 14 years leading the center, no renovation had required the Kennedy Center to close for even a day; outside of emergencies such as major snowstorms and the September 11 attacks, it remained open. A capital plan requiring a two-year shutdown carries “mammoth implications” for the institution during the closure and for its ability to recover afterward, he said: “That’s why the board would have to be deeply involved with it.” Kaiser sees a “terrible imbalance” at an institution that once relied on hundreds of trained professionals to operate its theaters, produce thousands of performances, and raise and earn millions of dollars annually. Now the staff is down to a skeleton crew. “It’s a chicken-or-egg question: Are they doing more because there’s no staff, or is there no staff because the board is doing more?” he said. “There’s no way a board of some 36 people can replace a staff of 700.” And there’s not much the law can do in the meantime, either. After Cooper’s May ruling, Trump threatened to step away from the center altogether—a death-by-neglect scenario that Lutnick said was still possible if Trump can’t renovate the building during his term. Barring some kind of political breakthrough, the only likely change that could end the stalemate might be one that nobody can hurry along: the end of Trump’s presidency, in 2029.

items.title: Incendies en Algérie : 123 feux en 24 heures, cinq toujours actifs
items.description: La vague d’incendies meurtriers continue de déferler sur les régions de l’Est de l’Algérie, mais elle a perdu de son intensité. Dans un point de situation publié sur Facebook, la Protection civile a indiqué avoir enregistré 123 feux de forêt depuis hier, dont 118 ont été éteints et cinq étaient toujours en activité ce samedi 29 août à 7 h 00 du matin. Les feux ont ravagé le couvert végétal, dévoré les habitations et anéanti le bétail. La région la plus touchée par cette catastrophe sans précédent reste Jijel où de nombreux morts et blessés ont été enregistrés. Cinq incendies toujours en activité à Jijel, Sétif et Tébessa Deux jours après cette tragédie, le danger rôde toujours, mais la situation sur le terrain s’est stabilisée. Cinq foyers sont toujours en activité. Les avions bombardiers d’eau sont venus en appui pour renforcer l’action des pompiers sur le terrain. Sur le front de la lutte contre les incendies, la Protection civile a fait état de 123 incendies, dont 118 ont été éteints et cinq toujours actifs, dont deux à Jijel, 2 à Sétif et le cinquième dans la wilaya de Tébessa. Incendies à Jijel : des familles évacuées de Texenna Dans le même communiqué, on apprend qu’un feu de forêt s’est déclaré dans la commune de Texenna, au secteur de Mechta El Messa. La région est connue pour son relief montagneux et ses forêts denses. Par mesure de précaution, des familles ont été évacuées. Deux avions AT 802 ont été mobilisés pour prêter main-forte aux sapeurs-pompiers. Une fois le danger écarté, les habitants ont pu regagner leurs domiciles. Les opérations se poursuivent sans relâche jusqu’à l’extinction totale des foyers recensés. Les conditions climatiques, marquées par de fortes chaleurs et des vents soutenus de ces derniers jours, ont favorisé la propagation rapide des flammes. La vigilance est plus que jamais de rigueur afin d’éviter que pareil scénario catastrophique ne se reproduise. L’article Incendies en Algérie : 123 feux en 24 heures, cinq toujours actifs est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: CM Afridi vows tougher child protection laws in KP after 5-year-old girl's rape, murder
items.description: HARIPUR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Saturday said the culprits involved in the rape and murder of a five-year-old girl in Haripur would be given exemplary punishment, adding that the Child Protection and Welfare Act was being made more stringent and renamed after the victim. The girl went missing from outside her home in Haripur on August 10. Her body was recovered on August 24 from an unused well at a warehouse about a furlong from her home on the information provided by one of the four suspects arrested in the case. Speaking to the media after offering his condolences to the girl’s family in Haripur on Saturday, CM Afridi vowed: “I assure you that whatever their [the suspects’] ages are, we will make an example out of them so that anyone committing such a beastly act will shudder before even thinking about it.” He said the KP Child Protection and Welfare Act would be named after the minor girl and assured her family of support from the provincial government in bringing the culprits to justice. The chief minister described the crime as inhumane and an act of savagery. “If our government and administration cannot protect our children from the criminals who are committing such sins without any fear, we should close down our offices — there is no use for them,” he said. CM Afridi directed the district administration, particularly the police, to further strengthen its writ to protect citizens of all ages. He also appealed to the judiciary to avoid granting relief to those involved in such incidents. “For God’s sake, do not give any relief to such criminals,” he implored. The chief minister again assured the victim’s father of the provincial government’s full support and appeared visibly emotional while consoling the man. According to PTI’s provincial chief whip, MPA Akbar Ayub Khan, the chief minister also announced financial assistance and a government job for the father. He further said that the Government High School for Girls in Pathan Colony would be renamed after the victim and announced a Rs2 billion Safe City cameras project for Haripur city.

items.title: Christians in India fear that tighter laws target them
items.description: Those going to church on Sunday in Mumbai will take part in an uneasy new ritual before the service. They will sign a form declaring that they are attending the service voluntarily and are not being forced to go to church or convert to Christianity. Around 4,000 churches in the Mumbai Metropolitan Area in the western Indian state of Maharashtra have decided to collect such “consent forms” to protect themselves ahead of an upcoming anti-conversion law that criminalises alleged forced conversions. “These consent forms are the least safety measure we can take to protect us from legal proceedings if anyone attempts to accuse the pastors or churches of forcibly converting people,” Dolphy D’souza, spokesman for the Bombay Catholic Society, told The Straits Times . “There have been a dozen disruptions of prayers in the past six months, by Hindu right-wing groups under the pretext of exposing forced conversions. So we have also asked churches to install CCTV cameras to identify attackers,” he added. The defensive actions in Mumbai are the latest response to a range of allegedly discriminatory actions by the Indian government against the Christian community, which is the third-largest religious group in India and comprises 2.3 per cent of the population. These include anti-conversion laws in several states and the tightening of laws governing foreign funding of non-profit organisations, which could result in the seizure of assets such as schools and hospitals built with such donations. Representatives of the Christian community in Mumbai said they fear an uptick in vigilante attacks on churches from Aug 28, when Maharashtra’s anti-conversion law, the Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act 2026, came into force. The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government in the western state passed the law in July. With that, Maharashtra becomes the 13th of India’s 28 states to enact an anti-conversion law. As in other states, the Maharashtra law paves the way for enforcement against religious conversion through coercion, fraud or inducements. Anyone who wants to adopt another faith must inform the authorities 60 days in advance. If these rules are violated, church officials or individuals can be jailed for seven years. Twenty civil society organisations, including Christian ones, held a press conference on Aug 24 in Mumbai asking for the withdrawal of the law, which they said is an “intrusive regulation of personal choices” and impinges on an Indian’s right to practise and propagate their faith freely, guaranteed in the Indian Constitution. “Fraudulent or coercive religious conversions are already punishable under Indian criminal codes,” said D’souza. “Distinct anti-conversion laws cast aspersions on permitted activities as well. They are a political weapon to polarise people and give a handle to Hindu majoritarian groups to misuse to terrorise religious minorities. “We have seen right-wing elements unleash violence on Muslims in India through lynching, bulldozing of houses and blocking namaz prayers in public. Now, the targeting of Christians is also expanding — they disrupt prayer meetings, saying we are forcing Hindus to become Christians,” said D’souza, adding that church groups’ requests for protection from the police had fallen on deaf ears. The consent forms and CCTV cameras in Mumbai, D’souza added, are a result of “the trust deficit” between the community and the city police and could serve as evidence against any targeted litigation. Anti-conversion laws Anti-conversion laws have been in effect in some Indian states since the 1980s, but have become harsher and more widespread in the past decade as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP has won elections in more states. The authorities and hardline Hindu groups affiliated to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the ideological parent of the BJP, often “struggle to differentiate between persuasion and coercion”, said a lawyer and former Catholic priest in the north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, which passed an anti-conversion law in 2020. He spoke to ST on condition of anonymity to avoid retaliation. Legal aid groups estimate that there are around 200 ongoing cases against Christians in Uttar Pradesh under its anti-conversion law, and more than 800 people, including pastors and worshippers, have been arrested or detained. Shiv, a 30-year-old pastor from a village in Lakhimpur Kheri district in Uttar Pradesh, told ST that a group of people claiming to protect the Hindu religion burst into his nightly prayer meeting in January. As the 90 or so attendees fled in fear, the vigilantes threw water on the dinner that had been arranged for them. They also allegedly roughed up the pastor, the owner of the prayer house and some women attendees, while shouting Hindu slogans. An hour later, the police arrived, arrested Shiv and detained him for 26 hours before registering a complaint under the state’s anti-conversion law. “I have held prayer meetings for three years in the village. Mostly labourers, small farmers and poor families attend to get a few hours’ respite from their hard life. I don’t force anyone,” said Shiv, who was granted bail but has not held services since as he awaits trial. The Uttar Pradesh lawyer, who represents over three dozen accused across the state, said that a year ago, the disruptions used to be at rural fellowships, but “now, extremist groups are targeting city churches as well”. Charitable work, educational assistance and religious preaching are often counted as “allurement” and brought within the scope of anti-conversion investigations, he added. A common slur used by Hindu right-wing trolls online against Christians is “rice bag convert”, which assumes that the person or his ancestors became Christian in exchange for these inducements. Several police complaints ST has seen simply list the Bible and cross under evidence to suggest coerced baptisms. Anti-conversion laws disproportionately impact women, young adults, Dalits (so-called lower-caste members) and tribals, who are assumed to be gullible and incapable of exercising independent choice, a press note issued by Mumbai civil society organisations said. Political commentator Insiyah Vahanvaty and Ashish Bharadwaj, professor and dean at BITS Pilani Law School, wrote in The Hindustan Times that while the anti-conversion laws claim to protect the vulnerable, their real-world impact is chilling. “Vigilantes use them to harass interfaith couples, suppress minority rights and instil fear in them… Claims of guarding against deceitful conversions ring hollow when couples marrying across faiths are arrested, or when volunteers handing out food are accused of enticement,” they wrote. The non-profit Citizens for Justice and Peace has challenged the validity of anti-conversion laws across Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh in a petition in the Supreme Court. On Oct 17, 2025, the court quashed five police complaints against 90 accused, including pastors from Fatehpur in Uttar Pradesh and hospital staff and university officials in Prayagraj, who were named in complaints of mass conversions of Hindus to Christianity in April 2022. The judges noted that “the criminal law cannot be allowed to be made a tool of harassment of innocent persons”, based on “completely incredulous material”. Targeting Christian non-profits The Indian government has also tried since March 2026 to pass an amendment to the 1970s Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) regulating the foreign funding of Indian non-profits and charities. The new bill allows a government authority to take over, manage or dispose of assets such as land and buildings funded by foreign sources when a non-profit’s five-year FCRA licence is suspended, cancelled, or not renewed. Christian-run non-profits were the first to demand changes to the Bill, backed by governments in states with significant Christian populations, such as Nagaland, Mizoram, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. Home Minister Amit Shah met concerned groups in early August and assured them that the amendment was “religion-neutral”. He added that the government had “no intention to harass the Christian community”, whose non-profits receive less than 15 per cent of total foreign donations. The government FCRA dashboard shows that more than 22,400 of the 52,000 registered charities have had their licences to receive foreign funds cancelled, and 15,200 licences have expired or not been renewed. Non-profits say they are rarely given clear reasons for cancellation or non-renewal. The official data does not classify how many of these are Christian or religious charities. But the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India and the National Council of Churches in India expressed concern that, as Christian organisations run thousands of schools, hospitals, and orphanages that rely on foreign donations, they were bound to be affected. Archbishop Joseph D’souza, president of the All-India Christian Council, described the amendment as “legalised loot(ing) of the Indian Christian community”. The developments have been criticised by politicians in the US. On Aug 5, Representative Riley Moore called India’s amendment a “clear attack on Christians”. In June, Senator James Risch, who heads the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, had described the proposed amendments as “deeply concerning”. In May, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s diplomatic itinerary to India included a highly publicised visit to the Missionaries of Charity headquarters in Kolkata, whose FCRA licence the Indian government had temporarily revoked in 2021 citing, vaguely, “adverse inputs”. A few days before Rubio’s visit, Representative Chris Smith wrote in an editorial in the Washington Examiner that impending changes to the FCRA could grant the Modi government sweeping powers to retroactively seize properties, schools and hospitals belonging to foreign-funded non-profits if their administrative licences are made to lapse. India’s Ambassador to the US Vinay Mohan Kwatra defended the amendments on social media as an attempt to improve transparency. He said that foreign contributions received by registered organisations in India had increased from US$1.2 billion (S$1.5 billion) in 2010-2011 to US$2.67bn in 2024-2025. But critics said tighter controls could make it harder for legitimate organisations to access overseas funding, and the government would be overreaching in taking over assets built with approved donations. “Non-profits would have used the donations to build schools, a small clinic, a toilet in a school or buy some equipment for a science lab, or a jeep to go to villages,” said John Dayal, a Delhi-based human rights activist and member of the National Integration Council of India, which works for religious harmony. “These are legitimate investments in community welfare made with legally obtained funds – seizing them retrospectively is to rob the poor communities they are meant for.” Facing criticism from politicians in the US, with whom India has yet to finalise its trade deal, the government on Aug 12 referred the Bill to a 31-member joint parliamentary committee for review. Dayal hoped the government would remove the “draconian” portions, but was not optimistic: “They may polish the language, but given the wider environment of the Modi government’s impatience for the concerns of religious minorities and critics, it is unlikely to change.” A development professional who works with some Christian-run non-profits in south India said that amid the tightening laws and uncertainty, those with most to lose were the three million civil society workers and volunteers, and needy communities. “Most non-profits work in the least developed districts of India, focusing on health, education, nutrition, livelihood, water access and disability. When the government closes the funding that keeps this going or takes over the assets, under newer and newer pretexts of transparency when they have all the information already, they are increasing the suffering of India’s most vulnerable,” she said. This article originally appeared in The Straits Times , an ANN partner of Dawn.

items.title: India's javelin champion Neeraj Chopra ends season early after ligament tear
items.description: Former Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra has ended his 2026 season early after sustaining a ligament tear during training, the javelin thrower announced in an Instagram post on Saturday. The 28-year-old Indian, who took gold at the Tokyo Olympics and won silver in Paris, placed second in the Lausanne Diamond League with a throw of 88.05 metres last week, but suffered the injury soon after, getting sidelined for a long period for the second time in a year. “After discussions with my doctor and team, we’ve decided that I will sit out the rest of this season,” Chopra posted. “It’s disappointing, especially because I felt close to finding my rhythm. But as they say, setbacks are a part of the journey.” View this post on Instagram Chopra, who had been dealing with lower back discomfort since 2023, aggravated a disc injury in September 2025 during training. Later that month, he went into a nine-month rehabilitation period after the Tokyo World Championships , and returned in June. He had qualified for the Diamond League finals set for Brussels next month. “My focus now is on recovering well and coming back even stronger,” Chopra added. The Tokyo Olympic champion, Chopra, and his successor in Paris, Pakistan’s Arshad Nadeem, faced each other in the World Athletics Championships in Tokyo in September last year. However, the highly anticipated clash of the South Asian titans failed to gain momentum in the sold-out Japan National Stadium, where Keshorn Walcott from Trinidad and Tobago won his maiden world title.

items.title: What Might Happen to Trump’s Ill-Gotten Gains
items.description: Americans are not accustomed to learning lessons about democracy from Nigeria, Peru, or the Philippines. That disregard may soon change. Those countries offer examples of what it looks like to reclaim stolen or swindled wealth from fallen authoritarian rulers. Done right, this work can deliver justice and strengthen democratic institutions for the long run. But cleaning up after a corrupt regime also comes with serious challenges and hazards. The Trump presidency has often looked more like a post-Soviet or postcolonial regime than like a first-world democracy. The Trump post-presidency may look the same. Trump has abused his office to enrich himself and his family in ways that are completely unprecedented—not only in the United States but also in the history of almost any peer democracy. Only Silvio Berlusconi, Italy’s notoriously lawless former prime minister, was in any way comparable, and Berlusconi was sentenced to prison. Trump faces little danger of prison. The U.S. Supreme Court has bestowed substantial criminal impunity on him, even assuming that he leaves office in 2029 as required by the Constitution. But an ex-president remains subject to civil liability, and the proceeds of bribery, extortion, insider trading, and market manipulation may be exposed to civil penalties. Other countries have shown the way. Alberto Fujimori, who was elected president of Peru in 1990, entered office at a time of extreme national crisis. The murderous Shining Path insurgency controlled much of Peru’s hinterland and terrorized the capital, Lima. Inflation ran at nearly 8,000 percent. Food and electricity were in constant shortage. Fujimori stopped the inflation and crushed the insurgency, but his harsh and sometimes criminal methods included warrantless detentions and extrajudicial killings. Fujimori dissolved Congress and the Supreme Court and rewrote Peru’s constitution to allow his own reelection in 1995. He won roughly two-thirds of the vote in a free, more or less, election. [ Philippe Sands: How far does Trump’s immunity go? ] But as Fujimori was doing things Peruvians wanted done, he was also presiding over a secret scheme of self-enrichment. His intelligence chief, Vladimiro Montesinos, operated a system of embezzlement and kickbacks that amassed hundreds of millions of dollars in foreign bank accounts. When this deception came to light, just after Fujimori’s 2000 reelection to a third term, he fled the country and resigned from office. To claw back these funds, Peru created a special prosecutor’s office and worked closely with the countries that hosted these contested assets. Peru has since recovered about $200 million of misappropriated wealth from accounts in the Cayman Islands, Switzerland, the United States, and Luxembourg, according to the database of the World Bank’s Stolen Asset Recovery Initiative. Peru’s economy also grew strongly after Fujimori’s fall from power. Foreign investment returned when the country renewed the rule of law. But then, in the 2010s, world demand slowed for Peru’s mineral exports, ensuring that Peru’s economy slowed too. Political instability returned. As Peru rotated through eight presidents over the past decade, a mood of “Fujimori nostalgia” gained strength. Fujimori’s daughter Keiko, who was elected to Congress in 2006, founded her own political party in 2010, built mostly on a message of family revenge and redemption. She ran for president in 2011, 2016, and 2021, losing narrowly each time. She ran again this year—and won. Believers in free and fair government can hope that Peru’s democratic institutions have strengthened sufficiently over the past quarter century to deter Keiko Fujimori from indulging in the deviousness that led to her father’s disgrace. But her tenure is new, and her political message has long been one of excusing her father’s abuses. Peru is not the only case of a former kleptocratic ruling family returning to power on a message of revenge and redemption. The Filipino dictator Ferdinand Marcos pillaged billions of dollars over two decades, from 1965 to 1986. After his ouster, his democratically elected successor, Corazon Aquino, created a Presidential Commission on Good Government to recover this stolen wealth. As of 2022, the PCGG had returned $5 billion to the Philippines, according to reporting by the country’s leading English-language newspaper. But as in Peru, proof of a former president’s corruption did not discredit his dynasty. In 2022, Marcos’s son—Ferdinand Marcos Jr., also known as “Bongbong”—was elected president. The PCGG still exists, but its work has ceased. The restored dynasty has reportedly returned to its corrupt ways, facing allegations of kickbacks as well as no-bid and no-work contracts, including more than $9 billion in devious government flood-control deals. Yet Bongbong Marcos has thus far respected the 1987 constitution adopted after his father’s dictatorship, which safeguards an independent judiciary and imposes an absolute ban on presidential reelection following a single six-year term. A big test for democracy in the Philippines is what happens in 2028. [ Casey Michel: America has never seen corruption like this ] The single most ambitious program of asset recovery has taken place in Nigeria. In the five years that Sani Abacha ruled the country as a military dictator, from 1993 until his death, in 1998, he stole perhaps $4 billion, stashing the funds in foreign accounts and shell companies. Revelations of his corruption discredited his military regime. In 1999, Nigeria returned to an elected government, which created a specialized unit in 2002, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, to reclaim these funds from Abacha’s heirs. This work received considerable help from the Swiss government, which agreed to freeze Abacha-related accounts, and from the United States, which cracked down on Abacha-owned shell companies. Nigeria got back about $1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s tally. In Nigeria, the Abacha name has become synonymous with fraud and crime. If you receive scam letters from Nigerian fraudsters, you’ll notice how often they impersonate a member of the Abacha family and promise access to hidden millions if only these funds could be moved to a trusted bank account. For this reason, the Abacha family has not enjoyed next-generation political success in Nigeria. The ex-dictator’s son has run for governor of the family’s home state of Kano a couple of times, including this year, but never got close to winning. But as Nigeria dissolves into conflicts along religious, ethnic, and regional lines, many Nigerians yearn for a “strong leader” in the Abacha mold. The country’s successful reclamation of wealth from Abacha’s heirs has also bred a new cynicism about the country’s democratic institutions, because so much of this money has been “re-looted” by Nigeria’s post-Abacha elected governments, especially by officials in President Muhammadu Buhari’s administration. The message to Americans? The recovery of corrupt assets from fallen leaders is not hopeless, but it is difficult and risky. This work demands permanent institutions specifically tasked to investigate and prosecute, and broad international cooperation to locate, identify, seize, and return dirty money. Even so, most people generally believe that the Fujimori, Marcos, and Abacha families kept much—if not most—of their corruptly obtained wealth. More dangerous, not every citizen will agree that the out-of-office autocrat should be brought to justice. The former leader’s followers, and especially his children, may convert complaints about imperfect justice into fuel for their own corrupt restoration. The fortunes, the fame, and the followings bequeathed by corrupt rulers to their heirs can support authoritarian power grabs long after the corrupt ruler departs this Earth. If the Trump family can keep the money it has accumulated this term, the next generation of Trumps will be far richer than Donald Trump ever was until his 80th year. Americans traditionally let bygones be bygones after a president leaves office, on the theory that ex-presidents rarely cause much trouble. But money is power in politics, and dirty money needs power to protect itself from the law. As much as Americans may wish to forget the Trumps and their corruption after this presidency ends, the next generation of Trumps surely understands that political power is its surest defense against legal retribution. This makes recovering the Trumps’ wrongfully obtained wealth not only a matter of justice but also a matter of democratic survival.
